'ddflow --version' takes ~1.0 s and importing ddflow.surfaces.cli ~0.83 s (ddflow.api imports dominate), 'ddflow list/show' ~4.7 s on this loaded machine, so argcomplete-style per-TAB invocation would add 1-5 s per keypress. The derived index .ddflow/index.db-<code fingerprint> is plain sqlite: items(id,kind,title,state,needs,tags,...) 3488 rows, count query 0.0 s, openable read-only with stdlib sqlite3. data.claim: Yes, but narrower than 'merge lanes'. (1) The lock/time saving comes from sharing the gate RUN, which P-batch-gates already designs and decided (D-BG-1..10: one CI/unit_tests/standards run on the merge of path-disjoint members, line-sized reviews, ddmin culprit search, one-transaction fan-out); uniting two agents does not by itself cut suite-lock contention. (2) The new value is freeing the LANE: when the remaining gates are machine gates (ci, unit_tests, standards via roborev) the agent need not wait at all, so release-at-enqueue plus a deterministic integrator frees the lane with no context transfer; only agent-judgement gates (rubber_duck, critic, bug_hunt, dedupe) need an agent, and there one surviving lane can review a combined unit while the donor's context travels as a handoff capsule. (3) ddflow wait cannot be interrupted today in the needed way: it is a blocking log poll, the holder is told at heartbeat, release or complete and never interrupted (services/waits.py), an MCP wait gives no progress and was aborted at 1800 s (Bfc43dae5b9), --max-s is ignored (B-wait-lease-max-s-ignored), and a message to a busy agent is delivered only at its next tool round. The pieces exist: DX-watch-job (done) gives bounded waits with resume tokens that renew leases; a wake reason (ready, merge_offer, yield, message) and an inbox are the missing part.

data.claim: Not as planned. P-security-gate (SEC-gatedef, SEC-scanners, SEC-deps, SEC-policy, SEC-findings, SEC-cadence, SEC-e2e) covers known-pattern scanners (bandit or semgrep, gitleaks, pip-audit), dependency advisories, a policy checklist with a cross-family review lens, and filing findings as bugs. None of it is an agentic vulnerability hunt, so it would catch known classes but not the logic and design flaws a Mythos-style audit finds. The method can be reproduced with whatever strong models are available, because the method is the agent loop, not one model: threat-model the code, partition it into audit units, let the agent read, hypothesise (source, sink, preconditions, CWE class), run the code in an isolated sandbox with a reproducer, and report only what reproduces, with exploitation steps, a failing test and a suggested fix. ddflow already has the pieces to host this (review machinery with FINDING lines and triage, a sensitivity vocabulary done as SE-sensitivity, a per-item scratch worktree, the declared surface registry as an entry-point inventory, a cross-family reviewer rule, regression-test-or-not-closed bug rule). data.body: Press coverage of Mythos reports model-assigned severity wrong in 14 of 27 checked cases, most overstated, while reproduced reports were nearly all real: so a deterministic rubric (reachability from an untrusted source, privilege needed, impact class, exploit complexity, affected versions) sets severity from the reproducer's facts, the model's rating is advisory, and the operator confirms anything at or above the blocking severity (D-security-gate-scope: high and critical block). data.body: Research R-shell-completion-design; D-completion-scope (bash+zsh+fish, argcomplete optional extra, IDs from the sqlite index, offered at onboard/adopt). GENERIC BY CONSTRUCTION (operator 2026-10-29): a new command, option, choice, record kind or harness must be completed with ZERO completion code. Rules: (1) one source of truth: the argparse parser that build_parser() returns (declarative registry Params + the ~43 hand-written add_argument calls); the completion engine introspects it at TAB time and no command, option or choice is listed anywhere else; (2) the three shell scripts contain no command names; (3) value kinds (record ids, phases, gates, agents, paths) come from metadata on the argument (Param.complete, inferred by default from the argument's name and the RecordKind registry) so a new record kind or id-like argument is picked up automatically, and an argument that should not complete must say so in an explicit exemption list; (4) ratchet tests fail the build when a new argument cannot be completed or is silently skipped. Argcomplete starts ddflow per TAB (about 1 s), so COMP-ids-fast keeps that path import-light.

Per D-completion-scope and the GENERIC rule of P-completion: the tree is DERIVED, never written by hand. One walker over the argparse parser build_parser() returns (registry Params and the hand add_argument calls, SuggestingParser subclass, compat aliases, hidden old flags per _hide_from_abbreviation) yields commands, options, arity, choices and value kinds; argcomplete uses the same parser object. No list of commands, options or choices exists in completion code. Tests: a differential test walks every command path of the real parser and compares what the walker reports with argparse's own actions (nothing missing, nothing extra); hidden and compat flags are not offered.

Per D-completion-scope and the GENERIC rule: bash, zsh and fish activation scripts (argcomplete registration per shell, global activation or per-command) that contain NO command, option or choice names; they only call the one completion engine. Managed templates under ddflow/templates/completion, one per shell, each under 20 KB. Without argcomplete installed: a clear message and exit 0, never a broken prompt. Tests per shell where it is installed (bash -n/zsh -n/fish -n plus a scripted TAB through the engine), otherwise recorded unavailable. Verify with the installed argcomplete that --shell fish is supported before relying on it (probe, record the version). Regenerate golden snapshots, README tables and pins.

Per D-completion-scope and the GENERIC rule: IDs come from the newest read-only .ddflow/index.db-* file; the record kinds that can be completed come from the RecordKind registry and the index tables (items, bugs, lessons, research, decisions, memories, prompts, rules ...), not a hand list, so a new record kind completes automatically. argcomplete starts ddflow on each TAB, so the completer path must not import ddflow.api (startup ~0.8 s): short-circuit before heavy imports and measure the budget. Falls back to nothing if no index; falsifier: if the budget cannot be met, report it to the operator.

Makes completion of VALUES automatic for future commands (operator 2026-10-29: future commands and parameters must be supported automatically). Add an optional Param.complete (id:<record kind>, phase, gate, agent, state, path, dir, enum, none) to the declarative registry; when it is unset, infer it: choices -> enum, a parameter named item/phase/bug/lesson/... or an id positional of a record verb -> the matching id kind (taken from the RecordKind registry, so a new kind needs no edit), paths from the type. Hand-written add_argument calls (about 43 in surfaces/parsers) get the same through a one-line helper or a completer attribute on the action, no parallel table. Anything that must not complete is listed in an explicit exemptions file (like surfaces/exemptions.py) with a reason. RATCHET test: walk the real parser and fail when an argument has an id-like name or a closed value set and resolves to 'free text' without an exemption; adding a command with an id parameter then needs no completion change, and a forgotten declaration fails CI instead of silently not completing.

Per the GENERIC rule of P-completion: (1) differential test, per shell where installed: for every command path of the real parser the engine offers exactly the parser's subcommands, options and choices; (2) CANARY test: register a synthetic command, option, choice and id-like parameter in a test parser (and a synthetic record kind) and assert the engine completes them with zero completion-code changes; (3) the COMP-declare ratchet runs in CI; (4) every shell script parses (bash -n, zsh -n, fish -n where present, else unavailable); (5) latency budget for command and id completion; (6) run the slow scenarios and ddflow pins regenerate --check.

Research the potential and option for ddflow to use AHP (Agent Host Protocol) to integrate with vscode and other tools that supports it. Does it make sense for our tool at all?

data.claim: Not as a core feature now. AHP (Microsoft, open, draft v1.1.0 over v1.0.0, JSON-RPC over message port locally and WebSocket remotely) is a coordination layer between several CLIENTS and an agent HOST: the host owns authoritative session state, sequences actions with a serverSeq, lets clients reconnect with lastSeenServerSeq and replay, arbitrates conflicts such as competing tool-call confirmations (first wins), and speaks ACP or another protocol to the agents behind it. It deliberately does not cover how agents reason, tools or models. ddflow's job is the queue, leases, gates and records over MCP, and its planned lane transport is ACP (R-acp, D-acp-r2, P-acp): AHP sits above that layer and solves multi-client viewing and persistence of one live agent session, which ddflow's deterministic lanes (D-swarm-answers) do not need. ddflow already integrates with VS Code with no AHP: the vscode harness descriptor (.vscode/mcp.json under the 'servers' key, .github/hooks/ddflow.json, copilot instructions), and VS Code's extensions can contribute tools, MCP servers and custom agents to the Agent Host. Three roles considered: (A) ddflow as an AHP CLIENT of a VS Code Agent Host (drive or observe Copilot, Claude and Codex sessions hosted by 'code agent host'): plausible later as one more lane backend, value moderate, blocked by an unconfirmed ability of a third-party client to create sessions and by the draft status; (B) ddflow as an AHP HOST exposing its lanes to VS Code's Agents window: attractive for operator visibility and approvals, but a large build (ACP-to-AHP event mapping, authoritative state beside the event log, auth) on a moving draft and with no documented support for third-party hosts in VS Code; (C) nothing now, keep MCP plus hooks for VS Code and add a read-only VS Code view only if wanted. Recommendation: C now, a small watch-and-probe task under P-acp for A, and revisit B when the spec is stable and VS Code documents third-party hosts.
data.falsifier: If a third-party client can create sessions on 'code agent host', attach to a running Copilot, Claude or Codex session and receive its events, and if VS Code's Agents window accepts a foreign host, role A becomes a cheap lane backend for hosted agents and role B an inexpensive visibility feature, and the recommendation changes to schedule them. If AHP reaches a stable 1.x with third-party hosts documented, revisit B.
data.mechanism: Sources read: VS Code docs agent-host concept page, the AHP doctrine and AHP-and-ACP pages, the AHP site index. Facts: standalone host 'code agent host' (localhost, connection token on by default, --tunnel to expose); adapters named for Copilot, Claude and Codex; third-party agent support not documented; client actions named in the pages: chat/turnStarted (send a turn), chat/toolCallConfirmed, chat/turnCancelled, sessions as URI channels with replay; session creation by a client is not described except that any client can start an automation run; SDKs in TypeScript, Rust, Kotlin, Swift, Go and .NET; the protocol says breaking changes may still be necessary while it is under active development. ddflow facts: ddflow/harnesses/vscode.toml (MCP path .vscode/mcp.json key servers, hooks style claude file .github/hooks/ddflow.json, injects session_start); P-acp has 21 open tasks (AC-spike wave 2 drives claude-agent-acp, codex-acp and opencode acp headlessly, AC-events maps session/update to ddflow events, AC-backend plugs the lane backend interface); lane decisions are D-swarm-answers (deterministic scheduler, pull lanes); operator approvals today go through the chat route.

Then record a decision: role A (ddflow as AHP client, one more lane backend behind AC-backend), role B (ddflow as AHP host exposing lanes to VS Code), or nothing; re-check when the spec leaves draft. Share the throwaway-script approach and the sandbox rules with AC-spike; unavailable tools are recorded unavailable, never passed.
